goals: Define the Industrial Revolution and say where and when it began
Explain the causes of the Industrial Revolution and why it began in England
Name the main inventions and describe the changes the Industrial Revolution brought

slides.heading: The Industrial Revolution: meaning, causes and inventions
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what changed, why in England, and with which machines.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning and dates of the Industrial Revolution, why it began in England, the inventions, and the changes it brought
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we learn what the Industrial Revolution was and where and when it began. We study the causes, and why England came first. We meet the main inventions of the textile industry, of iron and of power. Finally we see the changes that the Industrial Revolution brought to industry, transport and society.

slides.heading: What was the Industrial Revolution?
slides.body_md: Learn this definition well; it is the first part of many exam answers.

rows: A change from hand production in homes and workshops to machine production in factories
From about the 1750s or 1760s to about the 1830s or 1840s

visual.alt: Table on the Industrial Revolution: a change from hand production in homes and workshops to machine production in factories, using water and then steam power, beginning in England from about the 1750s or 1760s, lasting to about the 1830s or 1840s, and then spreading to other countries

slides.narration: The Industrial Revolution was a change from hand production in homes and workshops to machine production in factories. The machines were driven first by water power and then by steam. It began in England and later spread to other countries. It changed industry, transport and society.

slides.heading: When and where
slides.body_md: Use **about** with these dates; historians give approximate ranges.

visual.alt: Flow: the Industrial Revolution begins in England about the 1750s and 1760s, the first phase is complete about the 1830s and 1840s, and it then spreads to other countries
visual.caption: When and where.

slides.narration: The Industrial Revolution began in England from about the seventeen fifties or seventeen sixties. By about the eighteen thirties or eighteen forties the first phase was complete. After that it spread to other countries. Always use the word about with these dates, because historians give approximate ranges.

slides.heading: From the cottage to the factory
bullets: Before: the **domestic system**, work at home with hand tools.
After: the **factory system**, machines driven by power.
Workers now worked at fixed hours, under a master.

rows: Hand tools, hand wheel, hand loom
Families working at their own pace
Workers under fixed hours and a master

visual.alt: Table comparing the domestic system with homes, hand tools, human and animal strength and families at their own pace, with the factory system of large mills, machines, water and steam power and workers under fixed hours

slides.narration: Before the change, many families spun and wove at home with hand tools, at their own pace. This is called the domestic system. In the factory system, machines driven by power stood in large mills, and workers kept fixed hours under a master. This contrast is a useful way to explain the meaning.

visual.alt: Causes web: Why England first, at the centre, with ten boxes around it: capital, coal and iron, colonies, cheap labour, canals and roads, spirit of invention, navy and shipping, political stability, banking system and farming
visual.caption: Causes of the Industrial Revolution in England.

slides.narration: Look at the web. Ten causes worked together to start the change in England. They are capital, coal and iron, colonies, cheap labour, canals and roads, a spirit of invention, a navy and shipping, political stability, a banking system, and farming changes. No single cause explains everything.

slides.heading: Capital, colonies and banks
bullets: **Capital** from trade and colonies could be invested.
**Colonies** supplied raw materials such as cotton and were **markets**.
The **Bank of England** (1694) and other banks lent money.

rows: Merchants had money to invest in mills, machines and ships
Supplied raw materials such as cotton, and were markets for finished goods
The Bank of England (1694) and other banks lent money

visual.alt: Table of three causes: capital from trade and colonies for investment, colonies supplying raw materials such as cotton and markets, and the banking system including the Bank of England of 1694

slides.narration: First, capital. Merchants had made money from trade and colonies, and they could invest it in mills and machines. Colonies supplied raw materials such as cotton, and they were markets for finished cloth. The Bank of England, founded in sixteen ninety four, and other banks lent money to builders of mills.

slides.heading: Coal, iron and cheap labour
bullets: **Coal and iron** deposits lay **close together**.
The **enclosure movement** pushed rural people into towns.
They became **cheap labour** for factories.

nodes.label: Farm families lose access to the land

visual.alt: Flow: common land is fenced in the enclosure movement, farm families lose access to the land, they move to the towns, and they become cheap labour for factories
visual.caption: Enclosure and labour.

slides.narration: Coal and iron were found close together in England, so furnaces and engines could be supplied cheaply. Another cause was the enclosure movement. Common land was fenced into large private farms, and many farm families moved to the towns. There they became cheap labour for the new factories.

slides.heading: Shipping, stability and farming
bullets: A large **navy** and **merchant shipping** protected and carried trade.
**Political stability** encouraged investment.
An **agricultural revolution** fed a growing population.

rows: Protected trade routes and carried raw materials and goods
Steady government made owners willing to invest for the long term
Better farming fed a growing population, including town workers

visual.alt: Table of three causes: a large navy and merchant shipping protecting and carrying trade, political stability encouraging investment, and the agricultural revolution feeding a growing population

slides.narration: A large navy and merchant shipping protected trade routes and carried raw materials and goods. Political stability made owners willing to invest for the long term. And the agricultural revolution, meaning better farming, fed the growing population, including the workers of the new towns.

slides.heading: Canals, roads and the spirit of invention
bullets: **Canals and roads** moved coal, cotton and goods.
A **spirit of invention**: many people tried and patented new machines.

rows: Moved coal, cotton and finished goods between mines, mills and ports
Many people tried, improved and patented new machines

visual.alt: Table of two causes: canals and roads moving coal, cotton and goods, and a spirit of invention in which many people tried and patented new machines

slides.narration: Canals and roads moved coal, cotton and finished goods between mines, mills and ports. And there was a spirit of invention. Many people tried out, improved and patented new machines. In the next slides we meet the inventors one by one.

slides.heading: Inventions of the textile industry
slides.body_md: Cloth was the leading industry. Learn the machine, the inventor and the year.

rows: Spun thread by water power in mills

visual.alt: Table of five textile machines with inventor, year and use: flying shuttle by John Kay 1733, spinning jenny by James Hargreaves about 1764, water frame by Richard Arkwright 1769, mule by Samuel Crompton 1779, and power loom by Edmund Cartwright 1785

slides.narration: Cloth making led the way. The flying shuttle of John Kay, in seventeen thirty three, sped up weaving. The spinning jenny of James Hargreaves, about seventeen sixty four, spun several threads at once. Richard Arkwright built the water frame in seventeen sixty nine. Samuel Crompton made the mule in seventeen seventy nine, and Edmund Cartwright the power loom in seventeen eighty five.

slides.heading: Iron, steam and the railway
slides.body_md: Power and iron made factories possible anywhere, and railways joined the towns.

rows: Fast rail for goods and people

visual.alt: Table of iron, power and transport: Abraham Darby smelting iron with coke about 1709, James Watt improved steam engine patent 1769, George Stephenson locomotive Rocket 1829, and the Liverpool to Manchester railway of 1830

slides.narration: Abraham Darby smelted iron using coke, about seventeen hundred and nine, which made iron cheaper. James Watt improved the steam engine, with a patent in seventeen sixty nine, so power no longer depended on rivers. George Stephenson built the locomotive Rocket in eighteen twenty nine, and the Liverpool and Manchester railway opened in eighteen thirty.

slides.heading: What the Industrial Revolution changed
slides.body_md: Three areas: industry, transport and society.

rows: Factories, machines, mass production of cloth and iron goods
Growth of factory towns; new classes of owners and workers

visual.alt: Table of changes: industry with factories and mass production, transport with canals, roads and railways, and society with factory towns and new classes of owners and workers

slides.narration: The Industrial Revolution changed industry, transport and society. Factories and machines made goods in large numbers. Canals, roads and then railways improved transport. In society, factory towns grew, and new classes of owners and workers appeared. These changes lead into the next two topics.

Many causes worked together, from capital and colonies to coal and iron. The inventions of Kay, Hargreaves, Arkwright, Crompton, Cartwright, Watt, Darby and Stephenson drove it forward.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Begin with the **definition**, then the place and the **dates**, using **about**.
Group the causes: **money**, **materials**, **people**, **transport**, **government**.
Give the **inventor and year** together, for example **Kay, 1733**.
Do not mix up the **water frame** (1769) and the **mule** (1779).
For ten marks, give one clear point for each mark.

decks.title: Capitalism and Socialism: Part 2 — Meaning, Rise and Comparison
goals: Explain the meaning of capitalism and the causes of its rise
Explain the meaning of socialism and how the conditions of workers led to its rise
Distinguish capitalism from socialism on six points, without ranking them

slides.heading: Capitalism and socialism
slides.body_md: Part 2 — two economic systems, how each arose, and how they differ.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: capitalism, its meaning and rise, the conditions of workers, socialism and its thinkers, and a comparison of the two
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we study two economic systems. We learn the meaning of capitalism and why it rose after the Industrial Revolution. We study the conditions of workers, and how they led to the rise of socialism. Then we compare the two systems.

slides.heading: What is capitalism?
slides.body_md: An economic system with **private ownership** of the means of production.

rows: Land, factories and machines (the means of production) are privately owned
Set by market demand and supply

visual.alt: Table on capitalism: privately owned means of production, production for profit, prices set by demand and supply, competition between producers, and workers paid wages

slides.narration: Capitalism is an economic system in which the means of production are privately owned and run for profit. The means of production are land, factories and machines. Prices are set by market demand and supply. Producers compete for customers, and workers are paid wages.

slides.heading: Why capital mattered
bullets: Factories and machines **cost a great deal**.
Large **capital** was needed.
Investors, banks and companies supplied it.

nodes.label: Factories and machines cost a great deal
Investors, banks and companies supply it

visual.alt: Flow: factories and machines cost a great deal, so large capital is needed, investors, banks and companies supply it, and capitalism grows
visual.caption: Why capital mattered.

slides.narration: A factory with machines and engines cost far more than a spinning wheel in a cottage. So large capital was needed. Investors, banks and companies supplied it, and the system based on private capital grew. This is the first cause of the rise of capitalism.

slides.heading: Causes of the rise of capitalism
slides.body_md: Learn these six causes; any three or four usually earn full marks.

headers: Cause of the rise of capitalism
rows: Factories and machines needed large sums
Merchants and entrepreneurs put profits back into business
Pooled the savings of many people
Grew in size and put its money into business
Ideas of limited state interference spread

visual.alt: Table of six causes for the rise of capitalism: the need for capital, investment of profits, banks and joint-stock companies, trade and colonies, the growth of the middle class, and ideas of free trade and laissez-faire

slides.narration: Six causes are commonly given. The need for capital. The investment of profits by merchants and entrepreneurs. The growth of banks and joint stock companies. The expansion of trade and colonies. The growth of the middle class. And the spread of ideas of free trade and laissez faire.

slides.heading: Joint-stock companies
bullets: A company **sells shares** to many investors.
Each shareholder **risks only the sum paid**.
Large capital is gathered for mills and machines.

nodes.label: Many investors each pay a part
Each risks only what he or she paid

visual.alt: Flow: a company sells shares, many investors each pay a part, large capital is gathered, and each shareholder risks only the amount paid
visual.caption: A joint-stock company.

slides.narration: A joint stock company sells shares to many investors. Each pays a part, so a very large sum can be gathered. Each shareholder risks only the amount paid for the shares. In this way, mills and machines that no single owner could afford were built.

slides.heading: Free trade and laissez-faire
bullets: **Free trade**: few controls on trade.
**Laissez-faire**: the state interferes as little as possible.
Adam Smith's **The Wealth of Nations** (1776): remember the title only.

rows: Trade with few controls or duties
The state interferes as little as possible in trade and business
The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith, 1776 (title only)

visual.alt: Table: free trade means few controls, laissez-faire means as little state interference as possible, and the book named is The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith of 1776

slides.narration: Ideas of free trade and laissez faire spread. Free trade means few controls on trade. Laissez faire means that the state interferes as little as possible in trade and business. A book often named with these ideas is The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith, published in seventeen seventy six. You need to remember only its title.

slides.heading: Quick check: shares in a mill
slides.body_md: Which feature of the growth of capitalism is shown?
slides.narration: Read about the Tanwick Cotton Company. Decide which feature of the growth of capitalism the company shows.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: from scene to feature
slides.body_md: Read the scene, find the key words, name the feature.
bullets: Step 1 — What is happening?
Step 2 — Is it about rivals, profit, prices or pay?
Step 3 — Name the feature of capitalism.
Step 4 — Write one line of explanation.

rows: Two bakers of Tanwick lower their prices to win customers
Tobias Garn invests his profit in two more mills
Wool is scarce, so woollen cloth costs more and weavers make more
Prices set by demand and supply
A mill owner pays his weavers a weekly wage

visual.alt: Table sorting four imagined scenes to features of capitalism: lowering prices is competition, investing profit is the profit motive, scarce wool raising prices is demand and supply, and weekly pay is wages

slides.narration: Use four steps. See what is happening. Decide whether it is about rivals, profit, prices or pay. Name the feature of capitalism and write one line of explanation. Two bakers lowering prices show competition. Prices that move with scarce wool show demand and supply.

slides.heading: What is socialism?
slides.body_md: An economic system or idea of **ownership or control by society or the state**.

rows: The means of production are owned or controlled by society or the state
To reduce inequality and share wealth more fairly

visual.alt: Table on socialism: means of production owned or controlled by society or the state, the aim of reducing inequality and sharing wealth more fairly, and often planning and welfare

slides.narration: Socialism is an economic idea about who should own or control factories, land and machines. Under it, society or the state holds that ownership or control. Its aim is less inequality and a fairer sharing of wealth, and it often relies on planning and welfare. Notice that the word planning is used here, where capitalism speaks of the market.

slides.body_md: The conditions of workers led some thinkers and workers to look for other ways.

visual.caption: From factory conditions to socialist ideas.

slides.narration: Look at the flow chart. In the early factory towns, workers faced long hours, low wages, unsafe machines, crowded slums and no job security. Children and women also worked in factories and mines. The gap between owners and workers widened. This led to socialist ideas, and also to trade unions and to laws.

slides.heading: Conditions of industrial workers
slides.body_md: Learn these conditions; they are the heart of the third topic.

rows: Often 12 to 16 hours a day, for low wages
In factories and mines, for less pay
A widening gap between owners and workers

visual.alt: Table of conditions of workers: 12 to 16 hours a day for low wages, child and women labour in factories and mines, unsafe machines, crowded slums and disease, no job security, and a widening gap between owners and workers

slides.narration: Workers often laboured for twelve to sixteen hours a day, for low wages. Children and women worked in factories and mines. Machines were unsafe. Families lived in crowded slums where disease spread easily. There was no job security. And the gap between owners and workers kept widening.

slides.heading: Quick check: a mill worker's letter
slides.body_md: Which condition does the letter show?
slides.narration: Read the imagined letter of a mill worker. Decide which condition of industrial workers it shows.

slides.heading: Early socialist thinkers
slides.body_md: Often called **utopian socialists**. One line each is enough.

rows: Ran New Lanark with houses, a school and shorter hours for workers
Wanted industry organised for the good of society as a whole

visual.alt: Table of early socialist thinkers: Robert Owen at New Lanark with houses, a school and shorter hours, Saint-Simon wanting industry organised for society, and Fourier proposing small cooperative communities

slides.narration: The early socialist thinkers are often called utopian socialists. Robert Owen ran a mill community at New Lanark with houses, a school and shorter hours. Saint Simon wanted industry organised for the good of society as a whole. Fourier proposed small cooperative communities. One line for each is enough in an exam.

slides.heading: Marx and Engels
slides.body_md: Name the works and state the idea of class struggle neutrally.

rows: They argued that classes with opposed interests, owners and workers, shaped history

visual.alt: Table on Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto of 1848, Das Kapital first volume of 1867, and their argument that classes with opposed interests shaped history

slides.narration: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto in eighteen forty eight. Marx wrote Das Kapital, whose first volume appeared in eighteen sixty seven. You need to know only the titles and the dates. They argued that society had classes with opposed interests, owners and workers, and that the struggle between classes shaped history.

slides.heading: Trade unions and Factory Acts
slides.body_md: Workers and the law also responded to the conditions.

rows: Associations of workers who bargained together for wages, hours and safety
Laws; the Act of 1833 limited child labour in textile factories and provided for inspectors

visual.alt: Table of responses: trade unions of workers bargaining for wages, hours and safety, and Factory Acts, such as that of 1833 limiting child labour

slides.narration: Workers also responded by forming trade unions. These were associations of workers who bargained together for wages, hours and safety. The law responded too. The British Factory Act of eighteen thirty three limited child labour in textile factories and provided for inspectors. Remember this Act with its year.

slides.narration: Use the tables on the early thinkers and on Marx and Engels. Match each name with the right description.

Step 2 — What is the aim: profit or social welfare?
Step 3 — Who decides output: the market or a plan?
Step 4 — Name the system.

slides.narration: Here is the comparison on six points. Ownership: mainly private in capitalism, society or the state in socialism. Motive: profit, or social welfare. Prices and output: the market, or planning. Income: market returns, or a more even sharing. The state: limited, or larger. Competition: central, or less stressed.

slides.heading: Merits, criticisms and a mixed economy
slides.body_md: Describe both with their merits and criticisms. Do not rank them.
bullets: Each has supporters and critics.
Many countries, including India, follow a **mixed economy**.

rows: Incentives, choice, new ideas, growth of output
Security, fairness, planning for social goals
Inequality of income and insecurity of workers

visual.alt: Table of merits and criticisms: supporters of capitalism point to incentives, choice, new ideas and growth, critics to inequality and insecurity; supporters of socialism point to security, fairness and planning for social goals, critics to weaker incentives and heavy planning

slides.narration: Each system has supporters who point to its merits and critics who point to its limits. Supporters of capitalism point to incentives and choice, and critics to inequality. Supporters of socialism point to security and fairness, and critics to weaker incentives. Many countries, including India, follow a mixed economy.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: planning a 10-mark comparison
slides.body_md: Question: (i) Ownership and motive. [3] (ii) Prices, output and income. [3] (iii) State, competition, merits and criticisms. [4]
bullets: (i) Ownership and motive, one line for each system.
(ii) Market or plan; how income is shared.
(iii) State and competition; one merit and one criticism of each.

rows: Ownership and motive of each system
Prices and output; distribution of income
State, competition; a merit and a criticism of each

visual.alt: Table planning a ten-mark comparison: part (i) ownership and motive for 3 marks, part (ii) prices, output and income for 3 marks, part (iii) the state, competition, and a merit and a criticism of each for 4 marks

slides.narration: Plan a ten mark comparison in three parts. Part one compares ownership and motive. Part two compares how prices and output are decided and how income is shared. Part three compares the role of the state and competition, and gives one merit and one criticism of each system. Describe both sides evenly.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

sections.heading: 1. Meaning, dates and the change from home to factory
sections.body_md:
- **Industrial Revolution:** the change from **hand production in homes and workshops** to **machine production in factories** using power (**water**, then **steam**).
- It began in **England** from about the **1750s or 1760s**, continued to about the **1830s or 1840s**, and then **spread to other countries**.
- It changed **industry, transport and society**.
- Before: the **domestic system**; after: the **factory system**, with fixed hours under a master.

Machine production in large mills under fixed hours.

sections.heading: 2. Why England: the causes
sections.body_md:
- **Capital** from trade and colonies, and a **banking system** (**Bank of England, 1694**).
- **Colonies**: raw materials (for example cotton) and markets.
- **Coal and iron** deposits **close together**.
- **Cheap labour**: the **enclosure movement** and farming changes pushed rural people to towns.
- A large **navy** and merchant shipping; **political stability**.
- An **agricultural revolution** fed a growing population.
- **Canals and roads**; a **spirit of invention**.
- No single cause explains it; many worked together.

key_terms.definition_md: Fencing of common land into large private farms.
Money and resources available to invest in business.
Better farming methods that raised food output.

sections.heading: 4. Capitalism: meaning and rise
sections.body_md:
- **Capitalism:** an economic system in which the **means of production** (land, factories, machines) are **privately owned** and run for **profit**; **prices** set by market **demand and supply**; **competition**; workers paid **wages**.
- **Causes of its rise** after the Industrial Revolution: factories and machines needed **large capital**; merchants and entrepreneurs **invested profits**; **banks and joint-stock companies** grew; **trade and colonies** expanded; the **middle class** grew; ideas of **free trade and laissez-faire** spread (Adam Smith, **The Wealth of Nations**, **1776**: title only).

sections.heading: 5. Socialism: meaning and rise
sections.body_md:
- **Socialism:** an economic system or idea of **social ownership or control** (by society or the state) of the **means of production**. Its **aims** are to **narrow inequality** and to **share wealth more fairly**; it often relies on **planning and welfare**.
- **Conditions of workers:** **12 to 16 hours** a day and **low wages**; **child and women's labour** in factories and mines; **unsafe machines**; **crowded slums and disease**; **no job security**; a **widening gap** between owners and workers.
- **Early (utopian) socialists:** **Robert Owen** (New Lanark), **Saint-Simon**, **Fourier**.
- **Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels:** **The Communist Manifesto** (**1848**); Marx's **Das Kapital** (first volume **1867**). They argued that classes with opposed interests, owners and workers, shaped history (**class struggle**).
- **Trade unions**; Britain's **Factory Acts**, for example **1833**, limited child labour.

sections.heading: 6. Capitalism and socialism compared
sections.body_md:
- Compare on **ownership**, **motive**, **how prices and output are decided**, **distribution of income**, **role of the state**, and **competition**.
- Supporters of each system point to its **merits**, and critics to its **limits**. A history answer describes both side by side and does not rank them.
- Many countries, including **India**, follow a **mixed economy**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing dates without the word about, or placing the start in the nineteenth century.
- Mixing up the water frame (Arkwright, 1769) and the mule (Crompton, 1779), or the jenny and the power loom.
- Listing an effect, such as slums, as a cause of the Industrial Revolution.
- Confusing laissez-faire (limited state interference) with planning.
- Quoting books instead of naming them; only the titles and the main idea are needed.
- Declaring one system better; describe features, merits and criticisms of both.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or date.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a link, reasons or a comparison.

questions.stem_md: A poster outside the imagined Marlbeck Museum announces an exhibition called From Workshop to Factory. Which statement best defines the Industrial Revolution that the exhibition describes?

options.text_md: The spread of printing presses across the towns of Europe in the fifteenth century
The change from hand production in homes and workshops to machine production in factories, using power such as water and then steam
A short political uprising by workers in one English city
The discovery of new sea routes between Europe and Asia

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The change from hand production in homes and workshops to machine production in factories, using power such as water and then steam. The Industrial Revolution was the change from hand production to machine production in factories using water and then steam power. The other options describe printing, a political event and voyages of discovery, which are different developments.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Dunmere Debating Club, a speaker says that the Industrial Revolution began in England in a particular period and carried on to about the 1830s and 1840s before spreading to other countries. According to the usual account, when did it begin?

options.text_md: From about the 1450s
From about the 1850s
From about the 1900s
From about the 1750s or 1760s

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** From about the 1750s or 1760s. The usual account places the beginning in England from about the 1750s or 1760s. The 1450s are too early, and the 1850s and 1900s are after the first phase had already ended.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined village of Ashgrove, the open fields where families once grazed their animals are fenced into a few large private farms. Many labourers lose their access to the land and walk to the town of Marlbeck to look for factory work. Which development, and which cause of the Industrial Revolution, does this describe?

options.text_md: The enclosure movement, which supplied cheap labour to the towns
The Bank of England, which supplied capital to merchants
The flying shuttle, which speeded up weaving
The Factory Act, which limited child labour

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The enclosure movement, which supplied cheap labour to the towns. Fencing common land into private farms was the enclosure movement, and it pushed many rural people into towns, giving factories cheap labour. The Bank of England, the flying shuttle and the Factory Act do not describe the loss of access to land.

questions.stem_md: Surveyors in the imagined Greywater valley of northern England report that seams of coal and beds of iron ore lie only a few miles apart, so furnaces and engines can be supplied cheaply. Which cause of England's early industrialisation does their report show?

options.text_md: Colonies that supplied raw cotton
A large navy and merchant shipping
Coal and iron deposits found close together
The Bank of England of 1694

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Coal and iron deposits found close together. Coal and iron lying close together is a cause on its own. Colonies, shipping and banking are other causes, but the surveyors' report is about minerals found near each other.

questions.stem_md: A banker in the imagined port of Tanwick tells a visitor that merchants and manufacturers can borrow money more easily because England has a central bank founded in 1694. Which institution does he mean?

options.text_md: The East India Company
The Royal Navy
The Bank of England
A county court of the shire

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Bank of England. The Bank of England was founded in 1694 and was part of the banking system that helped industry. The East India Company was a trading company, the Royal Navy was the fleet, and a county court was a court of law.

questions.stem_md: A cloth maker in the imagined port of Tanwick buys raw cotton shipped from overseas colonies and sells her finished cloth to buyers in those same colonies. Which two advantages of colonies does her trade show?

options.text_md: Colonies supplied raw materials and also served as markets
Colonies supplied coal and iron ore and also trained English engineers
Colonies supplied capital through the Bank of England and also built canals
Colonies kept England politically stable and also fed its growing population

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Colonies supplied raw materials and also served as markets. Raw cotton coming in and finished cloth going out show colonies as a source of raw materials and as markets. The other pairs mention advantages that the cloth maker's trade does not show.

questions.stem_md: A museum label in the imagined Marlbeck Hall reads: This device of 1733 let a weaver send the shuttle across the loom far more quickly than by hand. Which inventor and machine does the label describe?

options.text_md: James Hargreaves and the spinning jenny
Richard Arkwright and the water frame
Edmund Cartwright and the power loom
John Kay and the flying shuttle

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** John Kay and the flying shuttle. The flying shuttle was invented by John Kay in 1733. The spinning jenny (about 1764), the water frame (1769) and the power loom (1785) came later and belong to other inventors.

questions.stem_md: A spinner in the imagined Marlbeck workshop can spin only one thread at a time on her hand wheel. A new machine of about 1764 lets one worker spin several threads at once. Which machine is this?

options.text_md: The steam engine of James Watt
The spinning jenny of James Hargreaves
The power loom of Edmund Cartwright
The Rocket of George Stephenson

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The spinning jenny of James Hargreaves. Spinning several threads at once is the spinning jenny of Hargreaves, about 1764. Watt's engine gave power, the power loom wove cloth, and the Rocket was a locomotive.

questions.stem_md: A timeline card in the imagined Dunmere museum reads: 1769, a spinning machine driven by water power, patented by Richard Arkwright. What was it called, and why did it suit a factory rather than a cottage?

options.text_md: The water frame; it was driven by water power, so it was set up in a mill beside a river rather than in a cottage
The spinning mule; it was driven by hand, so it was set up in a cottage
The power loom; it wove cloth by steam power, so it needed a mill
The flying shuttle; it was worked by hand, so it was kept at home

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The water frame; it was driven by water power, so it was set up in a mill beside a river rather than in a cottage. The water frame of 1769 needed a source of water power and was therefore placed in mills. The mule dates from 1779 and was not the 1769 machine, the power loom is from 1785, and the flying shuttle is from 1733.

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined coal pit at Greywater wants an engine that can pump water out of flooded tunnels and later turn the machinery of a mill without depending on a river. Whose improved engine, patented in 1769, served such purposes?

options.text_md: The locomotive of George Stephenson
The steam engine of James Watt
The coke furnace of Abraham Darby
The mule of Samuel Crompton

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The steam engine of James Watt. James Watt's improved steam engine (patent 1769) supplied power that did not depend on rivers. Stephenson built a locomotive, Darby smelted iron with coke, and Crompton's mule spun thread.

questions.stem_md: A poster in the imagined Dunmere railway hall shows a locomotive of 1829 and the opening in 1830 of a railway line between two English cities, Liverpool and Manchester. Who built the locomotive, and which kind of line opened?

options.text_md: James Watt; a railway between Liverpool and Manchester
George Stephenson; a canal between Liverpool and Manchester
George Stephenson; a railway between Liverpool and Manchester
Abraham Darby; a railway between Liverpool and Manchester

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** George Stephenson; a railway between Liverpool and Manchester. George Stephenson's Rocket (1829) was associated with the Liverpool and Manchester railway of 1830. Watt improved the steam engine, Darby smelted iron with coke, and the line in question was a railway, not a canal.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined village of Ashgrove around 1740, Anna spins thread on a hand wheel in her cottage, her husband weaves it on a loom in the next room, and a merchant collects the cloth every month. How should this way of working be classified?

options.text_md: Factory production driven by steam power
A joint-stock company raising capital from shareholders
A trade union bargaining for wages
Hand production at home, which factory production later replaced

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Hand production at home, which factory production later replaced. Spinning and weaving by hand at home is the older system that factories replaced. There are no machines driven by steam, no shares and no union in the scene.

questions.stem_md: A pupil at the imagined Dunmere school lists causes of the Industrial Revolution in England and, by mistake, includes one item that was a consequence of it rather than a cause. Which item is it?

options.text_md: Coal and iron deposits found close together
Capital from trade and colonies
The enclosure movement that sent people to the towns
The growth of crowded factory towns with slums

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The growth of crowded factory towns with slums. Crowded factory towns grew up because factories needed workers, so they were a result. Coal and iron, capital and enclosure all came before or helped to begin industrialisation.

questions.stem_md: A visiting lecturer at the imagined Dunmere Debating Club describes an economic system in which land, factories and machines are privately owned and run for profit, with prices set by demand and supply and workers paid wages. What is this system called?

options.text_md: Socialism
The domestic system
Capitalism
The guild system

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Capitalism. Private ownership of the means of production, the profit motive, market prices and wages describe capitalism. Socialism puts ownership with society or the state; the domestic system and the guild system were older ways of organising work.

questions.stem_md: To build a large mill and buy steam engines, the imagined Tanwick Cotton Company sells shares to many investors, each of whom risks only the money paid for the shares. Which feature of the growth of capitalism does this show?

options.text_md: The enclosure of common land
A joint-stock company raising large capital from many investors
A trade union bargaining for wages
A Factory Act limiting working hours

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A joint-stock company raising large capital from many investors. Selling shares to many investors to raise large sums is a joint-stock company, one of the ways capital was gathered. Enclosure, unions and Factory Acts are about land, workers and law.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined trade meeting in Marlbeck, a speaker argues that government should interfere as little as possible in trade and business and leave the market to itself. What is this idea called?

options.text_md: Laissez-faire
State planning
Guild control of wages
Enclosure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Laissez-faire. The idea of limited state interference in business is laissez-faire. State planning is the opposite approach, guild control belonged to an older system, and enclosure concerns land.

questions.stem_md: Tobias Garn, an imagined mill owner of Marlbeck, does not spend all his profits on himself but invests them in two more mills and new machines. Which cause of the rise of capitalism does his choice show?

options.text_md: The state decided what each mill should produce
Merchants and entrepreneurs invested their profits
Workers formed a trade union
A Factory Act reduced hours of work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Merchants and entrepreneurs invested their profits. Putting profits back into mills and machines is investment by an entrepreneur, a cause of the rise of capitalism. State decisions, unions and Factory Acts are not shown in the scene.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Tanwick cloth market, a fall in the supply of wool pushes up the price of woollen cloth, and several weavers decide to make more. Which feature of capitalism does this illustrate?

Production ordered by the state for the needs of all
Ownership of the mills by the whole community
Prices set by demand and supply in the market, which guide production

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Prices set by demand and supply in the market, which guide production. Prices moving with demand and supply and guiding what producers make is a feature of capitalism. The other options describe planning or collective ownership, which are features of socialism.

questions.stem_md: A speaker at the imagined Dunmere Debating Club describes an economic idea under which the means of production are owned or controlled by society or the state, with the aim of reducing inequality and sharing wealth more fairly. What is it called?

options.text_md: Socialism
Capitalism
Laissez-faire
The enclosure movement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Socialism. Ownership or control of the means of production by society or the state, with the aim of sharing wealth more fairly, is socialism. Capitalism and laissez-faire stress private ownership and limited state interference, and enclosure concerns land.

questions.stem_md: Edith Pell, an imagined mill worker of Marlbeck, writes home that she leaves before dawn and returns after dark, works about fourteen hours a day for low pay, and has no rest except on Sunday. Which condition of industrial workers does her account show?

options.text_md: Protection under a Factory Act
Job security under a written contract
Very long working hours and low wages
A share in the profits of the mill

questions.stem_md: A reporter writes about the imagined Orrin Falls mill, whose owner, like Robert Owen at New Lanark, provides houses and a school for workers' children and keeps hours shorter than elsewhere. Under which heading are such early thinkers usually placed?

options.text_md: Laissez-faire economists
Joint-stock investors
Early or utopian socialists
Enclosure landlords

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Early or utopian socialists. Robert Owen, Saint-Simon and Fourier are usually called early or utopian socialists. A mill owner who improves workers' lives is not a laissez-faire economist, a shareholder or an enclosing landlord.

questions.stem_md: A card in the imagined Dunmere library describes two French thinkers: one proposed small cooperative communities, and the other wanted industry to be organised for the good of society as a whole. Who are they?

options.text_md: Fourier and Saint-Simon
Marx and Engels
Arkwright and Crompton
Watt and Stephenson

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Fourier and Saint-Simon. Fourier proposed small cooperative communities and Saint-Simon wanted industry organised for society, and both are counted among the early socialists. Marx and Engels wrote later, and the other pairs were inventors.

questions.stem_md: A bookseller's imagined list in Dunmere shows two titles: one published in 1848 by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, and the first volume of another, by Marx, published in 1867. Which pair of titles is it?

The Communist Manifesto and Das Kapital

questions.stem_md: An imagined newspaper of 1833 from Marlbeck reports that a new law limits the employment of children in textile factories and provides for inspectors to visit the mills. Which law is this?

The Factory Act of 1833
The Peace of Augsburg of 1555
The charter of the Bank of England of 1694

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Factory Act of 1833. A law of 1833 limiting child labour in textile factories is the Factory Act. The other options belong to other subjects and dates.

questions.stem_md: Dock workers of the imagined port of Tanwick form an association so that they can bargain together for better wages and shorter hours. What is such an association called?

options.text_md: A trade union
A joint-stock company
A guild of merchants
A colonial council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A trade union. An association of workers that bargains for wages and hours is a trade union. A joint-stock company is owned by shareholders, a merchants' guild represents traders, and a colonial council governs a colony.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined class exercise at Dunmere school, one pupil writes: Means of production are privately owned, profit is the main motive and the market sets prices. The first describes capitalism and the second describes socialism

Both describe socialism

questions.stem_md: A quiz card at the imagined Dunmere Debating Club asks: India follows which kind of economy, one that combines features of both capitalism and socialism?

options.text_md: A purely market economy with no role for the state
A purely planned economy with no private business
A mixed economy
A domestic system of hand production

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A mixed economy. India follows a mixed economy, with both private enterprise and a role for the state. The other descriptions are extremes or an older system.

questions.stem_md: A pupil's imagined answer on capitalism and socialism ends with a closing sentence. Which closing sentence is acceptable for a history answer?

options.text_md: One of the two systems is clearly better, and the other has failed

questions.stem_md:
In the imagined town of Marlbeck, a lecture is advertised under the title Why England First?

(i) Define the Industrial Revolution and state when it began in England. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how capital, colonies, and coal and iron helped it to begin. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how labour, farming, banking, shipping and political stability helped. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and date; capital, colonies, coal and iron; labour, farming, banking, shipping and stability.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Industrial Revolution** was the **change from hand production in homes and workshops to machine production in factories**, using water and then steam power. It began in England from about the **1750s or 1760s**.

(ii) **Capital** from trade and colonies could be invested in factories. **Colonies** supplied raw materials such as cotton and also served as markets. **Coal and iron** lay close together, so furnaces and engines were supplied cheaply.

(iii) The **enclosure movement** and farming changes pushed many rural people to towns as **cheap labour**, and an **agricultural revolution** fed a growing population. The **Bank of England (1694)** supported lending, a large **navy and merchant shipping** protected and carried trade, and **political stability** encouraged investment.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Began from about the 1750s or 1760s in England

questions.stem_md:
The imagined debating club of Dunmere records three speakers on why industry grew first in England. Maud says that coal and iron explain everything. Peter says that colonies were the key. Ruth says that the new machines alone were enough.

(i) Name the cause that each speaker stresses. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the enclosure movement and the agricultural revolution contributed. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the claim that a single cause explains the Industrial Revolution. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Causes matched; enclosure and farming; evaluation of a single-cause claim.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Maud** stresses **coal and iron deposits found close together**. **Peter** stresses **colonies**, which supplied raw materials and markets. **Ruth** stresses **inventions**, the new machines.

(ii) The **enclosure movement** pushed many rural people into towns, where they became **cheap labour** for factories. The **agricultural revolution** raised food output, so a **growing population** could be fed and fewer people were needed on farms.

(iii) The claim is **only partly true**. Each cause mattered, but coal and iron needed **capital** and **banks**, machines needed **labour** and **markets**, and colonies needed **shipping**. Many causes worked together, so **no single cause** explains it.

questions.solution_md: Three textile inventions; Watt and Darby; the Rocket and other transport.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **flying shuttle** (John Kay, 1733), the **spinning jenny** (James Hargreaves, about 1764) and the **water frame** (Richard Arkwright, 1769); the mule (Crompton, 1779) and the power loom (Cartwright, 1785) are also correct.

(ii) **James Watt's** improved **steam engine** (patent 1769) gave power that did not depend on rivers, so mills could be built in towns. **Abraham Darby** smelted iron using **coke** (about 1709), making iron cheaper and plentiful for machines.

(iii) **George Stephenson's Rocket** (1829) was a locomotive, and the **Liverpool and Manchester railway** (1830) carried passengers and goods quickly. **Canals and roads** had already helped move coal, cotton and finished goods between mines, mills and ports.

(ii) Describe child and women's labour and the condition of workers' housing. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how these conditions led to ideas of socialism and to other responses. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Conditions; child and women's labour and slums; socialist ideas and other responses.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Workers faced **long hours**, often 12 to 16 hours a day, **low wages** and **unsafe machines**. Many also had **no job security**.

(ii) **Children and women** worked in factories and mines for low pay. Workers lived in **crowded slums**, where **disease** spread easily.

(iii) The **gap between owners and workers widened**, and some thinkers asked for a fairer sharing of wealth, so **early socialists** such as Owen, Saint-Simon and Fourier, and later **Marx and Engels**, put forward ideas of socialism. Workers also formed **trade unions**, and laws such as Britain's **Factory Act of 1833** limited child labour.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Widening gap leading to socialist ideas
(iii) Trade unions and Factory Act as responses

questions.stem_md:
A teacher at the imagined Dunmere school asks the class to prepare notes on socialism.

(i) What is meant by socialism, and what does it aim at? **[3]**
(ii) Write about Robert Owen, Saint-Simon and Fourier. **[3]**
(iii) Name the works of Marx and Engels, explain the idea of class struggle neutrally, and mention one response of governments to workers' conditions. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and aim; the early thinkers; Marx and Engels and a government response.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Socialism** is an economic system or idea in which the **means of production** are **owned or controlled by society or the state**. It aims to **reduce inequality** and share wealth more fairly, often with planning and welfare.

(ii) **Robert Owen** ran the mill community at **New Lanark**. **Saint-Simon** wanted industry organised for society, and **Fourier** proposed small cooperative communities. They are called early or utopian socialists.

(iii) **Marx and Engels** wrote **The Communist Manifesto** (1848), and Marx wrote **Das Kapital** (first volume 1867). They argued that society was divided into **classes with opposed interests** and that **struggle between classes** shaped history. Britain's **Factory Act of 1833** limited child labour.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Meaning: owned or controlled by society or the state
(ii) Owen, Saint-Simon and Fourier (one mark each)

questions.stem_md:
Two groups at the imagined Dunmere school prepare to compare capitalism and socialism as economic systems, each with its features, merits and criticisms.

(i) Compare the two systems on ownership and motive. **[3]**
(ii) Compare them on how prices and production are decided and on the distribution of income. **[3]**
(iii) Compare the role of the state and competition, and state one merit and one criticism claimed for each system. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Ownership and motive; prices, production and income; state, competition, merits and criticisms.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In **capitalism** the means of production are mainly **privately owned** and the motive is **profit**. In **socialism** they are **owned or controlled by society or the state**, and the aim is **social welfare**.

(ii) In capitalism **prices and production** are decided by the **market**, and income depends on market returns. In socialism they are guided by **planning**, and the aim is to **share income more evenly**.

(iii) The state has a **limited role** and competition is central in capitalism; the state has a **larger role** with planning and welfare in socialism. Supporters of capitalism point to **incentives and choice**, critics to **inequality**. Supporters of socialism point to **security and fairness**, critics to **less incentive and heavy planning**.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) A merit and a criticism for each, balanced

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined notice of a company and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Joint-stock company.

**(b)** Profit motive.

**(c) (i)** Many small sums made a large total.

**OR (c) (ii)** Private ownership; market prices.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A **joint-stock company**.

**(b)** The **profit motive**: production is run for profit.

**(c) (i)** Many people each paid a **small sum** for shares, so a **very large total** could be gathered for engines and machines that a single owner could not afford. This is how **joint-stock companies** helped the growth of capitalism.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Private ownership** by shareholders, and **prices set by the market**. Selling to buyers at home and in the colonies also shows expanding trade.

questions.passage_md:
**From an imagined notice issued by the Tanwick Cotton Company in the late 1700s**

The company will raise money by selling shares in the new mill at Tanwick. Any person may buy shares, and no shareholder can lose more than he or she has paid for them. The money will buy steam engines and spinning machines. The cloth will be sold at home and in the colonies, and the profits will be divided among the shareholders according to the shares they hold. The company expects the price of its cloth to be set by the market.

answer.model_answer_md: A **joint-stock company**.

children.stem_md: Which feature of capitalism is shown by the sentence about the profits?

answer.model_answer_md: The **profit motive**: production is run for profit.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which two features of capitalism, other than profit, can be seen in the notice?

answer.model_answer_md: **Private ownership** by shareholders, and **prices set by the market**. Selling to buyers at home and in the colonies also shows expanding trade.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined letter and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Unguarded machines.

**(b)** A Factory Act.

questions.passage_md:
**From an imagined letter of Edith Pell, a mill worker of Marlbeck, to her sister in the countryside, in the 1830s**

I work at the loom from before sunrise until after dark, nearly fourteen hours a day, and the pay is barely enough for bread. My youngest cousin, who is only nine, works beside me, and the machines have no guards. We sleep five to a room in a lane where the water is foul and fever is common. If I fall ill, there is no pay and no promise that my place will be kept. Our men have begun to meet in a union, and a new law has been spoken of, which may limit the work of children.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Orrin Falls mill, the owner owns every loom and keeps the profit from the cloth, while the weavers receive a fixed payment each week for their labour. Which feature of capitalism does the weekly payment show?

options.text_md: Prices are fixed by a planning committee
The mill is owned by the whole community
The state decides how much cloth is to be woven
Workers are paid wages

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Workers are paid wages. A fixed payment for labour is a wage, one of the features of capitalism. Planning committees, community ownership and state decisions on output belong to socialism, not to this mill.

questions.stem_md: A merchant of the imagined port of Tanwick complains that heavy duties and rules on his cargoes slow his business, and says he would prefer trade with few controls. Which idea that spread with the rise of capitalism is he supporting?

options.text_md: The domestic system
State planning of output
Free trade
The enclosure of common land

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Free trade. Preferring trade with few controls and duties is the idea of free trade, which spread along with laissez-faire. The domestic system, state planning and enclosure are different matters.

questions.stem_md: Two pupils of the imagined Dunmere school prepare notes on capitalism for a class display. Pupil 1 lists incentives, wide choice and growth of output as points that its supporters make, and inequality of income as a point that critics make. Pupil 2 writes that capitalism has no merits at all. Which judgement is sound for a history answer?

options.text_md: Pupil 2 is sound, because a system that has critics can have no merits
Pupil 1 is sound, because a history answer sets out the merits claimed by supporters and the criticisms made by critics
Both are sound, because any list of points is acceptable in history
Neither is sound, because history does not discuss economic systems

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Pupil 1 is sound, because a history answer sets out the merits claimed by supporters and the criticisms made by critics. A balanced answer reports what supporters and critics say. Pupil 2 dismisses the whole system, and the other options are wrong in claiming that criticism cancels every merit or that history ignores economic systems.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A librarian at the imagined Dunmere library says that The Wealth of Nations, linked with the ideas of free trade and limited state interference, was published in 1776.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations was published in 1776, and it is linked with those ideas. Only the title and date are needed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Joint-stock companies helped capitalism to grow after the Industrial Revolution.

**Reason (R):** Factories and machines needed far larger sums than a single owner could usually provide, and shares allowed many investors to contribute.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. The need for large capital, met by selling shares to many investors, is exactly why joint-stock companies helped capitalism to grow, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Orrin Falls, three rival cloth sellers cut their prices to win buyers, and each hopes to make a profit. Name two features of capitalism that this scene shows.
questions.solution_md: Competition and profit motive.

answer.model_answer_md: The scene shows **competition** between rival sellers and the **profit motive**. The falling prices also show that **prices respond to the market**, a further feature.
